title: Li Ning's resource endowment became a curse, while Jinjiang's grassroots shoe factories ran ahead
dek: Li Honggu said Li Ning is a company made of countless mismatches: its founder had no ambition for business, held resources no one could match, and those resources became a curse instead. Jinjiang's shoe factories were set up by Minnan farmers pooling household funds, carried no baggage, and made decisions only around the market — and over the long run they ran more steadily.
why: The industry-history section gives rare mechanisms: joint-household fundraising, "kill the pests, protect the flowers," and the "halfway up the mountain" theory; the second half has Li Honggu dissecting why Li Ning was overtaken and how capital became the new curse — the sharpest part.
who: Founders and investors in consumer brands, manufacturing, or family-business governance; anyone who wants to know why Li Ning and Anta took different paths.
skip: The Ding clan ancestral hall observations from 9:58 are more anecdote — fast-forward to the Nike contract-manufacturing line at 15:58.

points.h: Jinjiang is not the Fujian version of the Wenzhou model
points.body: Fei Xiaotong summed up China's rural development into four models: Sunan had government leading farmers to set up factories, Wenzhou relied on individual households, the Pearl River Delta relied on foreign capital plus labor for processing and assembly. Jinjiang appeared last and is the easiest to underestimate. It was not individual households but township enterprises set up by several families and relatives pooling funds, with a quasi-private shareholding character: in 1979, when Lin Tuqin set up Jinjiang's first shoe factory, he gathered 14 households of villagers to buy in — these people were both shareholders and employees; in 1982, when they wanted to start over, they also split from the original factory into five factories. The money came from Minnan's distinctive biao hui, in a gray zone of finance, and many companies that later grew big raised their early money this way. The local government also proposed the "five allows": allowing dividends, share-based fundraising, hiring workers, and sales commissions.

points.h: Under the fake-medicine case, the government chose to kill the pests and protect the flowers
points.body: Jinjiang had two early quality crises. One was "week shoes" and "street-crossing shoes": farmers didn't understand that shoes needed specialized glue, and used ordinary glue to stick soles to uppers, so they came apart after seven days — one consumer said they came apart just crossing the street. The second was the 1985 fake-medicine case: white sugar ground into powder and congealed into blocks, stuffed with white fungus to pass as granules, flowing through gray channels to hospitals, reported nationwide by People's Daily. Jinjiang goods became notorious, and over a thousand ground-promotion salesmen were turned away; some hotels threw their luggage out the door. At the time, Fujian's first provincial party secretary, Xiang Nan, was very market-oriented — he expanded the Xiamen special economic zone, borrowed international loans to build Xiamen airport, and called Chendai's workshops "a flower of township enterprises" — yet for this he was criticized as too far to the left, made five or six self-criticisms within half a year, and stepped down. As he left, he instructed the people handling the fake-medicine case: kill the pests and protect the flowers; when you pour out the bathwater, don't throw the baby out with it.

points.h: Li Ning's resource endowment became a curse instead
points.body: Jinjiang's shoe factories were all Nike's apprentices, but the first to develop the awareness of building a domestic brand was Li Ning. Li Ning founded its brand in 1990, collecting sacred flame beneath the snow mountains of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau and passing it nationwide, with enormous impact; the registration milestones of Jinjiang brands almost all come after this — Anta applied in 1990 and registered successfully in 1991, Peak was originally named Fengdeng and changed its name in 1990-1991, and 361° was previously called Bieke. But the two paths were completely different: Li Ning carried a national halo from its founding, and when performance doubled year after year in the mid-1990s it set the goal of spending ten or twenty years to put a Chinese brand in the world's number one position; its founder had no ambition for business and hired professional managers to run it, and as a result fell into crisis and internal friction again and again. Jinjiang brands were grassroots, had no historical baggage, and made all decisions around the market.

points.h: The family that gave away 51% hit every node
points.body: In 1988, Ding Shizhong was not yet 18, a middle-school dropout, and persuaded his father to give him 10,000 yuan to buy 600 to 700 pairs of shoes; he took a two-day, two-night hard-seat train to Beijing and became one of the first "Beijing drifters." Around the same time, Li Ning was wearing Li Ning-brand clothes carrying the Asian Games sacred flame in Beijing. He wanted to sell Jinjiang shoes into Xidan and Wangfujing, but those were powerful state-run department stores, and a 17- or 18-year-old kid from Fujian simply couldn't get in; it took him one or two years of grinding before he got a counter. Another easily overlooked point is his father, Ding Hemu: the only male in the family, his family was actually weak in the village — Minnan clans fought over land and factory buildings, relying on having many sons and on fists, and Ding Hemu didn't participate. He taught his son to give others more benefit in doing business: "give others 51% of the benefit, take only 49% yourself."

points.h: Inventory enough to clothe the whole nation for three years
points.body: Around 2000, Anta signed Kong Linghui and advertised on CCTV and became an overnight sensation; on top of the Sydney Olympics, the men's football team reaching the World Cup, and the successful Olympic bid, the whole industry frantically signed spokespeople and opened stores, with the peak year opening close to 1,000 stores. Peak founder Xu Jingnan's metaphor was "riding an elevator": a person standing still in the elevator still grows, and everyone thought that after the Beijing Olympics they would ride an even faster elevator. But two or three years after the Olympics the inventory crisis erupted: one manager described it as, even if Jinjiang's shoe factories stopped producing, the shoes in inventory would be enough to clothe the whole Chinese nation for three years. The root cause was the dealership model of enfeoffment plus futures — ordering half a year in advance, the brand too far from the market, and dealers unwilling to share real sales data. Anta's response was to strengthen centralization, with Ding Shizhong personally touring stores like an emperor on campaign, covering 400 to 500-plus market points in China in the worst one or two years.

points.h: The book is missing Nike and Adidas as the coordinate system
points.body: Li Honggu's biggest criticism of the book is that it lacks an implicit thread: Nike and Adidas's campaigns in the Chinese market actually determined the rises and falls of Chinese brands to a greater extent — they are the real coordinates. Huang Ziyi agrees, but explains that there is too little detailed material on Adidas and Nike's playbook, because multinational companies have to go through procedures and have discipline when giving interviews. Li Honggu also argues that Li Ning's problems cannot be explained by the professional-manager system: Li Ning is "a company made of countless mismatches" — he was not happy doing business, his resource endowment far exceeded everyone else's, yet it formed a huge gap with his vision and strategy, and the resources became a curse instead. And today, after Jinjiang brands obtained capital and acquired international brands, a new problem has appeared: how to tell a story of an international brand and oneself — "capital has become their curse."

points.h: Anta's multi-brand: independent front end, shared middle and back office
points.body: Anta's FILA was learned. Li Ning was the first to be overtaken by Nike in 2003 and lose the market's number one spot, and was the earliest to try multi-brand; Li Ning's first professional manager, Chen Yihong, also did KAPPA very well. When Anta acquired FILA, at first it likewise put traditional Anta products under the FILA label to sell, and only when they didn't sell did it painfully start over: in organizational structure and process, keep the FILA team absolutely independent from the Anta team, eliminate mutual influence, then poach a world-class team for design, move toward fashion and trends, and do DTC direct retail at the same time. Once it worked, Anta's multi-brand mechanism was: the retail end and the product design and R&D end each independent, sharing Anta's powerful middle and back office, including human resources, the contract-manufacturing system, and Jinjiang's industrial cluster. What Ding Shizhong now repeatedly says is: I don't want to make China's Nike, what I want to make is the world's Anta.

points.h: Once per-capita GDP passes $10,000, verticals take off
points.body: When Huang Ziyi interviewed Anta in 2021, an Anta vice president explained why it acquired Amer Sports, Descente, and Kolon: according to their research in European and American markets, when a country's per-capita GDP reaches $10,000, niche sports tracks begin to emerge — ice and snow, outdoor, hiking; when it reaches $20,000, these niche sports begin to flourish on a large scale. At the time of the interview, China had just broken through $10,000; now Beijing and Shanghai have already exceeded $20,000, and the national average is about $15,000, so these brands taking off may be a natural process. Where Anta is stronger than others is that it may, through a relatively advanced professional-manager consciousness, be the first to do market research and lock up these tracks.

terms.def: Jinjiang's local term for overseas remittances, vacant overseas houses, and surplus labor — the three raw conditions for setting up a factory.
Mutual-aid lending in Minnan's acquaintance society, in a gray zone of finance, and the startup capital source for early factories.
The policy proposed by Chendai and Jinjiang local governments: allow dividends, allow share-based fundraising, allow hiring workers, allow sales commissions.
When an enterprise reaches medium scale, if it can complete the modern-enterprise transformation it climbs further; if not, it may fall into the abyss.
The brand opens its own stores to reach consumers directly, bypassing layer upon layer of dealers.
Nike technology that knits an entire shoe upper from a single yarn, making sneakers light and breathable and overturning the leather-upper paradigm.
